propositions.text: The male claimant, his wife (the claimant), and their minor children are Chinese citizens claiming protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "male claimant"), his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "claimant" herein unless otherwise indicated) and their minor children, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are citizens of China. They claim protection under Sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

propositions.text: The allegations come from the amended common PIF Narrative of the adult female claimant in Exhibit C-2.
propositions.quote: ALLEGATIONS (From amended common PIF Narrative of adult female claimant (the "claimant" herein unless otherwise indicated) in Exhibit C-2):

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimants are Chinese citizens seeking protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97, based on the female claimant's amended PIF Narrative.

propositions.text: The claimant had her first daughter in 2004, had to wait 4 years and get a permit for a second child, was forced to wear an IUD, and had two forced abortions in 2006 and 2007.
propositions.quote: The claimant had her first daughter on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2004, and could not have a second child until she waited 4 years and got a permit. She was forced to wear an IUD, which she had problems with, and she was forced to have two abortions when it was discovered she was pregnant in XXXX 2006 and XXXX 2007.

propositions.text: She had a second daughter in 2009 and could not have more children.
propositions.quote: She had a second daughter in XXXX 2009, and could not have more children.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports the claimant's allegations of forced IUD use, two abortions, and birth restrictions between 2004 and 2009.

propositions.text: Each parent was to be sterilized but had medical problems; the male paid a 20,000 Yuan deposit and the female had to wear an IUD.
propositions.quote: Each parent was to be sterilized, but each had medical problems. He had to pay a 20,000 Yuan deposit and she had to wear an IUD.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports that both parents were to be sterilized but had medical issues; the male paid a deposit and the female wore an IUD.

propositions.text: In late 2011, they found the claimant was pregnant, went into hiding before a checkup, received notices for abortion, sterilization, and a large fine, and their home was damaged with a big fine ordered.
propositions.quote: In late XXXX 2011, they tested themselves and found out she was pregnant, so they went into hiding before the next checkup in early XXXX 2011. They heard that a notice was left for them to attend the appointment, then another notice for abortion and sterilization, and a large fine, because they believed she was pregnant again. The home was damaged and they were ordered to pay a big fine.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports the claimants hid after discovering pregnancy in 2011 and faced notices, fines, and home damage.

propositions.text: After the claimants left, the male claimant's mother was detained for a week and developed asthma.
propositions.quote: After they left the male claimant's mother was detained for a week, and she developed asthma.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports the male claimant's mother was detained and developed asthma after the claimants left.

propositions.text: They did not disclose their route through the USA to CBSA on snakehead's instructions and did not know Canadian immigration law, but later told the truth on their lawyer's advice.
propositions.quote: They did not disclose their route through USA to CBSA on instructions of the snakehead. They did not know Canada's immigration law, so they listened to the agent. Their lawyer in Canada told them to tell the truth, so they did

propositions.text: The claimants had their third child in 2011 and the claimant is pregnant again, fearing abortion, sterilization, and a large fine.
propositions.quote: The claimants had their third child in XXXX 2011, and she is pregnant again. They fear abortion, sterilization and a large fine.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports the claimants hid their USA route initially, later told the truth, had a third child in 2011, and fear forced abortion and fines.

propositions.text: The Panel finds the claimants are not Convention refugees under Section 96 as they lack well-founded fear of persecution on Convention grounds.
propositions.quote: The Panel finds the claimants not to be Convention refugees under Section 96, as they do not have a well-founded fear of persecution in China on any of the five Convention grounds.

propositions.text: The Panel finds the claimants are not persons in need of protection under Section 97 as removal would not subject them to risk of life, cruel treatment, or torture.
propositions.quote: The Panel also finds that the claimants are not persons in need of protection under section 97 as, on a balance of probabilities; their removal to China would not subject them personally to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture.

propositions.text: The Panel will provide reasons for these findings.
propositions.quote: The Panel's reasons are as follows.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97, and will explain reasons.

propositions.text: The Panel considered credibility and whether claimants require protection due to China's one child policy, applying Gender Guidelines.
propositions.quote: The Panel considered the issue of credibility. The Panel also considered whether the claimants require Canada's protection because of the potential application of the one child policy in China. The Panel applied the Gender Guidelines

paragraphs.summary: The Panel considered credibility and the one child policy's application, applying Gender Guidelines.

propositions.text: The Panel considered all evidence and submissions, including counsel's written submission dated March 4, 2014.
propositions.quote: The Panel has considered all of the evidence and submissions, including counsel's written submission, including of documents, dated March 4, 2014 (the "submission").

paragraphs.summary: The Panel considered all evidence and submissions, including counsel's March 4, 2014 written submission.

propositions.text: The claimant gave oral testimony; the male claimant agreed and added nothing; both adult claimants are equally subject to a negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: The claimant provided the oral testimony. The male claimant agreed with what his wife said, and declined to add anything. As the male claimant adopted what his wife said, and their PIF Narrative was joint, a negative credibility finding applies equally to both adult claimants.

propositions.text: The minors were excused after identification; the claim fails for all claimants due to the female claimant's lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: The minors were excused after being identified. Thus, as the claimant was found to be not credible, the claim fails with respect to all claimants.

propositions.text: Certain documents submitted are not genuine, negating credibility of both adult claimants presumed to have submitted false documents.
propositions.quote: The Panel will note below that certain document(s) submitted will be found to be not genuine, and that redounds to negate the credibility of both adult claimants, as both will have been presumed to have submitted the false document(s).

propositions.text: Both adult claimants are found not credible overall.
propositions.quote: Thus, both adult claimants are found to be not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds both adult claimants not credible, minors excused, and some submitted documents not genuine, causing claim failure.

propositions.text: The Chinese passports establish the claimants' personal and national identities; familial relationships are accepted from testimony.
propositions.quote: From the Chinese passports of all claimants in Exhibit R/A-2, the personal and national identities of these claimants are established. The Panel accepts from testimony the familial relationships alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel accepts the claimants' identities and familial relationships based on passports and testimony.

propositions.text: The claimant alleged being wanted by authorities but was allowed to exit China via agent's arrangement, which is unlikely but not disbelieved for credibility.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleged she was wanted by authorities when she left China. However, she indicated that, despite this, the family was allowed to exit through Chinese exit controls. When asked how this was possible, she said the snakehead, or agent, arranged it for them. While this is technically possible, it is very unlikely. However, as this is in the nature of an implausibility only, the Panel will refrain from making a negative inference as to credibility from this.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds the claimant's story of exiting China despite being wanted unlikely but does not negatively infer on credibility.

propositions.text: The claimant alleged two forced abortions; the Panel does not accept this for credibility reasons.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleged that she suffered two forced abortions between her first and second children. Had the Panel accepted this, then it is very possible her claim might have been accepted, for various reasons. However, for credibility reasons, the Panel does not accept this.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel rejects the claimant's allegation of two forced abortions due to credibility concerns.

propositions.text: The abortion certificates contain inconsistent ages; the claimant's explanations are not accepted; the documents are found not genuine.
propositions.quote: The translations of the certificates allegedly documenting these forced abortions are found on pp. 67 and 69 of Exhibit C-7. On p.69, the certificate in regard to the second procedure indicates the claimant to have been 31 years old on the date of the procedure, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2006. However, the claimant was born on XXXX XXXX, 1975 as per her passport. Therefore, she was 30, not 31, on XXXX XXXX, 2006, and the claimant was asked to explain this. She said it is Chinese custom or practice to enter in a document, say 31, if the patient is 30, or in her 31st year, as the claimant was then. However, it was pointed out to the claimant that on p.67, the certificate in regard to the second procedure indicates the claimant to have been 32 years old on the date of the procedure, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2007, and she in fact actually was 32 then, and 32, not 33, was entered. Thus, she was asked, why was this practice / custom only applied for once certificate, but not the other. Then she blamed this on mistake of the hospital. The Panel cannot accept this explanation. The claimant purports to rely on these documents to prove her claim, yet indicates they are not accurate, when challenged. This is the reason which causes the Panel to find these documents to be non-genuine. In making this finding that these documents are not genuine, the Panel notes that it is consistent with what is indicated in item 3.22 of Exhibit R/A-1, which references the proliferation of false documents emanating from China. A finding that a document is not genuine is sufficient to find the claimant, overall, to be not credible, and the Panel thus does so in this event.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds abortion certificates inconsistent and claimant's explanations unconvincing, concluding the documents are not genuine and negating credibility.

propositions.text: Because the abortion documents are not genuine, the female claimant did not suffer involuntary abortions and has less reason to leave China.
propositions.quote: From this also flows a finding that the female claimant did not suffer involuntary abortions, thus the claimants had much less of a reason to leave China.

propositions.text: The Panel will not apply the doctrine of Compelling Circumstances as the claimant did not suffer forced abortions as alleged.
propositions.quote: The Panel also for this reason will not apply the doctrine of Compelling Circumstances, as it conceivably could have considered, in that the Panel finds that the female claimant did not suffer two (or any) forced abortions as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds no forced abortions occurred and declines to apply Compelling Circumstances doctrine.

propositions.text: The abortion certificates' addresses match the claimant's 2009 address but she omitted earlier addresses from 2001 to 2009 without explanation.
propositions.quote: The Panel also noted the address of the claimant on the abortion certificates, in an effort to see if they matched the address of the claimant as given in s.11 of her PIF. They did match the address given as of 2009. However, for some reason, the claimant omitted to indicate what her address was from 2001 to 2009, including what her address was in 2006 and 2007, the relevant times.

propositions.text: The claimant could not explain the omission but the Panel will not make a negative inference, though notes a missed opportunity to validate the certificates.
propositions.quote: The claimant could not explain why she did this, only to say that the family moved for some nine months in 2009. All this is somewhat odd, but the Panel will not make a negative inference as to credibility, but will note that an opportunity was foregone to validate the alleged genuineness of these certificates.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel notes address omissions in the claimant's PIF but declines negative credibility inference, noting a missed chance to validate certificates.

propositions.text: Many documents, including abortion certificates, were sent from China in 2012, after claimant arrived in Canada in 2011.
propositions.quote: Many of the documents in Exhibit C-7, including the abortion certificates, were, as per the claimant, sent to her from China in 2012, and the envelope in which the documents were allegedly sent was shown at the hearing. However, the claimant arrived here in XXXX 2011,

propositions.text: The claimant did not bring these documents from China, saying she did not know they were necessary until consulting a Canadian lawyer.
propositions.quote: so, she was asked, why did she not bring these documents, valuable to prove her refugee claim, with her from China? Her answer was that she did not know they were necessary for her refugee claim, and she only got the idea when she spoke to her consultant in Canada.

propositions.text: This unusual explanation supports the finding that the documents are not genuine.
propositions.quote: This is unusual, and buttresses the finding above that the documents submitted are not genuine.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds it unusual that claimant received key documents from China after arriving in Canada, supporting their non-genuineness.

propositions.text: A medical document for the male claimant indicates 'chronic prostitutes' likely means chronic prostate problems; claimant said it healed in China in 2011.
propositions.quote: The allegation was made that the male claimant had medical issues, thus could not be sterilized. In support, a medical document for him was submitted, the translation being on p.51 of Exhibit C-7. It was divined at the hearing between counsel and the Panel that "chronic prostitutes" probably meant chronic prostate problems. The claimant explained that her husband had chronic prostate gland inflammation. Given that she said his problem was chronic, she was asked if he was taking any medication or medical attention for this condition in Canada, and she said it healed in China in 2011.

propositions.text: The Panel finds it unlikely a chronic condition healed shortly before coming to Canada, so medical documents are of lesser weight or not genuine.
propositions.quote: However, as the problem was said to have been chronic, the Panel finds that it would have been unlikely to have been healed shortly before the claimants came to Canada. Thus, the Panel attaches this part of the medical documentation submitted, and by inference the other medical documentation, allegedly sent from China at the same time, to be of lesser weight, if it is even genuine.

propositions.text: This applies also to the Notice of Sterilization document in Exhibit C-7.
propositions.quote: This analysis applies as well to the Notice of Sterilization, the English translation of which appears on p.63 of Exhibit C-7.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel doubts the male claimant's chronic medical condition healed before arrival, reducing weight of medical documents and sterilization notice.

propositions.text: The claimant changed the date of moving/hiding from 2011 to 2011 in PIFs; the Panel does not accept the explanation of mistake.
propositions.quote: The issue of the claimant's addresses was re-visited. The claimant indicated that they hid, and changed residences, out of fear, in XXXX 2011. However, their PIF's. s.11, originally indicated that they moved, or hid, as of XXXX 2011, and, as per Exhibit C-6, submitted shortly before the hearing, they changed this to XXXX 2011. The claimant was asked why they originally indicated they moved in XXXX 2011, and all she could say was that it was a mistake. However, the Panel does not accept this explanation, given the other credibility concerns herein.

propositions.text: The claimants confirmed their PIFs were true, correct, complete, understood, and translated before signing.
propositions.quote: The claimants confirmed when they signed their PIF's, and again at the outset of the hearing, that their PIF's were true, correct and complete, that they understood them, and that they were translated back into their language to them before they signed their PIF's.

propositions.text: The claimant now alleges the PIF was in error; the Panel makes a negative inference on credibility from this variance.
propositions.quote: Notwithstanding this, the claimant now alleges that the PIF was in error. Considering the other credibility concerns herein, the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility from the variance between the original version of the PIF, and the amended version.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel rejects the claimant's explanation for PIF date changes and infers negatively on credibility due to inconsistencies.

propositions.text: The claimant's PIF said they were ordered to pay a big fine, but at hearing she said the fine was verbal only; the Panel rejects this explanation and finds it implausible.
propositions.quote: The claimant indicated in her PIF Narrative that, when the claimants were in hiding, the PSB came to their residence and left notices, and they were "ordered to pay a big fine". However, at the hearing, the claimant indicated they were not ordered to pay a fine. When questioned on the inconsistency, the claimant said it was verbal only. The Panel does not accept this explanation for the inconsistency, as it actually does not explain it, and, also, the Panel finds it implausible that a significant fine would be levied by means of a verbal notice only.

propositions.text: The claimant submitted other notices allegedly from Chinese authorities but contends the fine was verbal only, which is not believable; the Panel makes a negative inference on credibility.
propositions.quote: The claimant has submitted other notices allegedly issued by the Chinese authorities to control and punish the claimants, yet contends that a significant fine was levelled, verbally only. This is not believable, and from this the Panel makes a negative inference as to credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds the claimant's inconsistent statements about a fine implausible and negatively infers on credibility.

propositions.text: The claimant alleged that the PSB damaged their home.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleged that the PSB damaged their home

propositions.text: The claimant provided no documentary evidence such as photos or invoices to prove the damage claim.
propositions.quote: but could provide no documentary evidence that this was done, such as photos, invoices for replacement, repair, etc.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleged PSB damaged their home but provided no documentary evidence, says the court.

propositions.text: The claimants were not forthright and admitted lying to Canadian authorities about their travel route.
propositions.quote: The above findings that the claimants have not been forthright are significantly fortified by the fact that the claimants, by their own admission, did not tell the truth to the Canadian authorities when they initially made their refugee claim in Canada.

propositions.text: In POE Notes, claimants said they flew directly from Hong Kong to Toronto, but later changed route in PIF to include USA stops and illegal crossing.
propositions.quote: In Exhibit R/A-2, the Port of Entry (POE) Notes, the claimants indicated to CBSA that they flew directly for Hong Kong to Toronto. However, later, in the PIF, they changed their route to indicate that they flew from Hong Kong to Los Angeles, then to Seattle, then crossed illegally to BC, then flew domestically from Vancouver to Toronto.

propositions.text: The claimant said the agent advised them to make false statements about their travel route.
propositions.quote: The claimant was asked why they made this false series of statements, and she said the agent advised them to do so.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimants admitted lying about travel route, initially saying direct flight but later admitting illegal US crossing, blaming an agent.

propositions.text: The claimant was a mature adult who knowingly lied to the Canadian government and the explanation blaming a smuggler is not accepted.
propositions.quote: The Panel does not accept the claimant's explanation that she felt she had to listen to a smuggler, a criminal

propositions.text: The claimants were not threatened by the smuggler at Immigration in Toronto and likely lied to avoid questions about not claiming asylum in the USA.
propositions.quote: They did not suggest the smuggler threatened them when they attended at Immigration, inland, in Toronto. Perhaps the claimants did not want to have to answer questions at their hearing about their failure to make an asylum claim in USA.

propositions.text: The claimant said counsel told her to tell the truth eventually.
propositions.quote: The claimant said her counsel told her to ultimately tell the truth.

propositions.text: The Panel finds claimants likely decided to admit the lie at PIF because CBSA had evidence they entered the US illegally.
propositions.quote: More likely, the Panel finds, the claimants probably decided to "come clean" at the PIF stage because they noted what the CBSA agent inscribed in s.21, IMM 5611, in the POE Notes

propositions.text: The Panel makes a negative credibility inference from the admitted lie and does not believe the claimant.
propositions.quote: from this admitted lie to the Government of Canada the Panel makes a negative inference as to credibility. If the claimant does not tell the truth, then the Panel simply does not believe the claimant, nor should the Panel.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects the claimant's smuggler excuse, finds they lied knowingly, and draws a negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: The claimant said they left China due to fear of abortion, sterilization, fines, etc.
propositions.quote: The claimant indicated that the left China due to fear of abortion, sterilization, fines, etc.

propositions.text: The claimant admitted being in the USA for days en route to Canada but did not claim asylum there, blaming the smuggler.
propositions.quote: they belatedly admitted they were in USA for a number of days en route to Canada, but did not make an asylum claim during their sojourn there, despite USA being a signatory to the 1967 Protocol

propositions.text: The claimant's illegal border crossing and failure to claim asylum in the USA indicate no genuine fear of return to China.
propositions.quote: she allegedly performed an illegal hike over an unfamiliar international boundary, risking apprehension, detention and potential removal to China on the way. The Panel finds that this behaviour indicated that the claimant did not have a real, or genuine, fear of a return to China as alleged.

propositions.text: The Panel draws a negative credibility inference and finds the claimant was asylum shopping or had a plan to bring family to Canada.
propositions.quote: Further, in that she alleged that she did, from this the panel makes a negative inference as to credibility. The Panel finds that the claimant was simply asylum shopping, or, in the alternative, embarked on a deliberate plan to get her entire family to Canada, for whatever reason.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's failure to claim asylum in the USA and illegal crossing show no genuine fear and draws a negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: Due to credibility issues, the claimant's evidence is overall not credible and insufficient to support refugee protection claim.
propositions.quote: From all the above credibility issues, the Panel finds that the claimant's evidence has been, overall, not credible, and thus insufficient to support the claimants' claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's evidence not credible and insufficient to support the refugee claim.

propositions.text: The claimants arrived in Canada in 2011 and have one Canadian child, expecting another in 2014.
propositions.quote: The claimants came to Canada in XXXX 2011. They have had one child here, a Canadian citizen now, and are expecting another future Canadian citizen child in XXXX 2014.

propositions.text: Counsel indicated the child will be born in Canada and the Panel agrees.
propositions.quote: Counsel indicated that this child will be born in Canada, and the Panel agrees.

propositions.text: The claimants claim the claimant will be persecuted if returning to China with two Canadian and two Chinese children.
propositions.quote: The claimants now claim that the claimant will be persecuted if she returns to China with two Canadian children in addition to her two Chinese children.

propositions.text: The Panel acknowledges some possibility of persecution in China for having more than one child.
propositions.quote: The Panel acknowledges that t here is some possibility of persecution in China in some circumstances if Chinese citizens have more than one child in China, or two in the case of the claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The claimants arrived in Canada in 2011, have two Canadian children, and claim persecution risk in China for having multiple children, acknowledged by the Panel.

propositions.text: There is some possibility of persecution in China for having more than one child, including two for the claimant.
propositions.quote: here is some possibility of persecution in China in some circumstances if Chinese citizens have more than one child in China, or two in the case of the claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds some possibility of persecution in China for having more than one child.

propositions.text: The Panel finds the state did not force the claimant to undergo abortions, despite it being conceivable.
propositions.quote: The Panel has found, for credibility reasons, that the state did not force the claimant to undergo any abortions. It is conceivable that such could have occurred to a person with the female claimant's profile, but the Panel finds that it did not occur to her.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds the claimant was not forced to undergo abortions despite it being conceivable.

propositions.text: The claimant and husband are 38 and 34 years old, making it less likely she will be sterilized near end of child-bearing years.
propositions.quote: Probably apropos of nothing, the Panel notes the claimant is 38 and her husband 34 as of the hearing, which would appear somewhat unusual. The female claimant is, as noted, 38 years old, and it may be less likely than otherwise that China will enforce sterilization on a female citizen relatively close to the end of her child-bearing years.

propositions.text: The claimants may decide to leave Canadian children in Canada, avoiding one-child policy issues in China.
propositions.quote: It is also possible that if the claimants do leave Canada, they may decide to leave their Canadian children in Canada, in which event they would have only the two Chinese children in China, and would thus not fall afoul of the one-child policy.

propositions.text: The Panel does not rely on speculation about future children or leaving children in Canada in its decision.
propositions.quote: However, again, the Panel does not rely on this factor in making its decision.

propositions.text: The Panel notes children 3 and 4 are Canadian citizens and not refugee claimants, so their issues in China are not the Panel's concern.
propositions.quote: Also not directly considered by the Panel is that in the hypothetical event children 3 and 4, the Canadian citizens, were brought to China by the adults (if China would even accept them as immigrants), then any problems they would hypothetically face could be said to not be the direct concern of the Panel, as these children are not refugee claimants before the Board, and thus are not directly entitled to Canada's refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel notes ages reduce sterilization risk, possible leaving Canadian children in Canada, and that Canadian children are not claimants.

propositions.text: Counsel argued the one-child policy applies fully to claimants even for children born outside China, with draconian enforcement in Guangdong.
propositions.quote: Counsel went to great efforts to point out to the Panel that the one-child policy would be fully in force against the claimants, regardless of the factors noted in the immediately preceding paragraph, and more importantly, regardless of the fact that children 3 and 4 would have been born outside China. She pointed out documentation which specifically indicates that in Guangdong Province, where the claimants are from and where they presumably would go to, the draconian policies of sterilization, abortion, serious fines, etc., apply to families where children are born outside China.

paragraphs.summary: Counsel argued the one-child policy applies fully to claimants even for children born outside China, with strict enforcement in Guangdong.

propositions.text: The Panel agrees the law applies but must consider if it is enforced.
propositions.quote: Thus, the Panel would have to agree with counsel that such is the state of the law. However, the Panel also needs to consider whether the law is actually being enforced.

propositions.text: Exhibit R/A-1 states people returning from abroad are welcomed and children born outside China are largely forgiven; rich citizens pay fines or travel abroad for more children.
propositions.quote: In general, people who return to China from abroad are actively welcomed back to the "motherland" and children born outside China largely forgiven ... Chinese couples living abroad are not bound to the one-child policy. Chinese citizens studying or working in foreign countries can return with more than one child without any serious problem ... Chinese nationals who have children while abroad may not be subject to the one-child policy ... there is an emerging class of rich Chinese citizens who simply pay a fine or travel overseas to have additional children.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel agrees the law applies but notes evidence that enforcement is lax for those returning from abroad, per Exhibit R/A-1.

propositions.text: Despite the law, claimants would not be persecuted if they returned to China with Canadian children, so no serious possibility of persecution exists.
propositions.quote: It thus appears as if, despite the letter of the law, the claimants would not be persecuted in China if they hypothetically returned there, and decided to take children 3 and 4 there and make the necessary efforts to allow these Canadian citizen children to gain entry to China, and the Panel so finds. Thus, the Panel finds, there is not even a serious possibility that any of the claimants would be persecuted in China, as these restrictive laws and policies would not apply to them.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds no serious possibility of persecution in China despite the law, if claimants returned with Canadian children.

propositions.text: For credibility reasons, the Panel finds claimants were not persecuted in China and submitted false documents and untruths to CBSA.
propositions.quote: For credibility reasons, the Panel has found that the claimants were not persecuted in China in the past. They submitted at least one false document, and admittedly made a significant untruth to CBSA.

propositions.text: The Panel does not accept the claimant's allegations about the Family Planning Office or future persecution in China.
propositions.quote: For this reason, the Panel does not accept that the Family Planning Office is looking for the claimant or has a file on her, as she alleges. For reasons noted above, the Panel also does not accept that any claimant will be persecuted in China upon a hypothetical return there.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel finds claimants not credible, not persecuted in China, and rejects allegations about Family Planning Office and future persecution.

propositions.text: The Panel finds claimants are not Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection and rejects the claim for all claimants.
propositions.quote: As a result of the above findings, the Panel finds the claimants to not be Convention refugees under section 96, nor persons in need of protection under section 97 of the IRPA. As such, for the reasons noted above, the claim is rejected with respect to all the claimants.

paragraphs.summary: The Panel concludes claimants are not refugees or in need of protection and rejects the claim.
